Nuclear Deterrence. During the Cold War, both superpowers developed a strategy to prevent war through the threat of mutually destructive nuclear retaliation, formalized as Mutually Assured Destruction, or MAD. The doctrine rested on an assumption that both sides would avoid war if both faced total annihilation. It required maintaining credible second-strike capability, the assured ability to retaliate even after absorbing a nuclear first strike. This strategy paradoxically became the principal mechanism preventing superpower conflict, even as it drove both sides to accumulate tens of thousands of weapons capable of ending civilization.

The doctrine emerged after the Soviet Union acquired atomic weapons in 1949. Both superpowers soon realized that neither could achieve nuclear superiority without triggering its own destruction. Maintaining second-strike capability created intense pressure to deploy missiles, bombers, and submarines constantly and globally. This dependence on always-ready retaliation generated technological arms races: ballistic missiles, submarine-launched weapons, and multiple independently targeted reentry vehicles, all pursued to maintain deterrent credibility.

The strategy assumed rational leaders would never initiate nuclear war knowing the outcome. But nuclear crises like the Cuban Missile Crisis revealed how miscalculation could trigger accidental war. Preventing such disasters required sophisticated early-warning systems, communication redundancy, and dispersed launch authority to prevent enemy decapitation strikes, creating complex bureaucracies of nuclear command and control. Critics argued that MAD was psychologically destabilizing and morally indefensible. Proponents credited it with preventing direct US-Soviet war despite decades of proxy conflicts and crises elsewhere.
